tidystata

tidystata is a set of functions that combines Stata-inspired features with tidyverse-style operations.

The package focuses on exploring and preparing data:

  • tab(), tab1(), and tab2() for frequency tables.
  • fre(), fre1(), and fre2() for frequency tables with totals.
  • summ() and tabstat() for summary statistics.
  • pwcorr(), misstable(), and tab2(.chi2 = TRUE) for correlations, missing values, and tests of independence.
  • codebook() and variables() for variable inspection.
  • isid(), duplicates_report(), assert(), is_first(), and s_merge() for checking keys and merging, and print_all() for listing every row.
  • s_select(), row calculations, conversion helpers, std(), pc(), as_dummy(), panel lags (s_lag(), s_lead(), s_diff()), and binning for data preparation.

tidystata 0.3.0 retires the import/export, regression-table, and detailed-codebook wrappers. See the migration guide for direct package alternatives and breaking changes. This experimental package is undergoing stabilization; see NEWS for changes in each release.

Installation

You can install the development version of tidystata like so:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("socimh/tidystata")

R 4.1.0 or later and a suitable build toolchain are required to install from source. Rich table formatting is optional and requires flextable.

If you already have this source repository on your computer, open tidystata.Rproj and restart R before installing the local changes:

devtools::install(".", upgrade = "never", build_vignettes = FALSE)

Restart R again, then check the version and installed location:

library(tidystata)
packageVersion("tidystata")
find.package("tidystata")

Opening the source folder alone does not change what library(tidystata) loads. Repeat the installation after editing source code. During package development, devtools::load_all(".") loads the working source into the current session; installation followed by a fresh R session tests the installed package.

Learn the workflow

Read Getting started for a small exploration and preparation workflow, and Containers and missing values for return types, grouping, labels and previews. In an installation that includes vignettes, use vignette("getting-started", package = "tidystata").

Coming from Stata? findit() gives the R equivalent of a Stata command. Type one Stata word bare, or quote anything longer; the usual Stata abbreviations work:

findit(reg)
findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)")
findit(left_join) # R functions work too

The Coming from Stata article lists every entry by topic, in English and Chinese, including the packages to use beyond tidystata.

Plain manual scripts are in the source repository’s examples/ folder. Open a script in your editor and run its lines individually; from a source checkout, source("examples/02_frequency_tables.R", echo = TRUE) runs a complete example. The full migration guide is on the website.

Table return types

Most table-producing helpers, including the tab, summ, codebook and variables families, preserve the input container by default: a tibble returns a tibble, a base data frame returns a base data frame, and a data.table returns a data.table. List outputs remain lists, with each table following the same rule. Explicit output options override this default. pwcorr(), misstable() and duplicates_report() always return tibbles, as their help pages state. Summaries and variable inventories are ungrouped; grouping columns are retained where the function normally reports them. Arbitrary data-frame subclass metadata is not guaranteed on newly constructed tables. Vector and scalar helpers retain their usual outputs.

preview_table() preserves the underlying container while changing its console display. unpreview_table() removes that display setting. External dplyr and tidyr verbs retain their own container and grouping behavior, with preview settings preserved for supported operations.

Example

Load the package

Load tidystata and the data-manipulation package used in these examples.

library(tidystata)
library(dplyr)

codebook()

View the codebook of lifeexp.

codebook(lifeexp)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 5
#>   variable  label                    type             n unique
#>   <chr>     <chr>                    <chr>        <int>  <int>
#> 1 region    Region                   double+label    68      3
#> 2 country   Country                  character       68     68
#> 3 popgrowth Avg. annual % growth     double          68     32
#> 4 lexp      Life expectancy at birth double          68     20
#> 5 gnppc     GNP per capita           double          67     64
#> 6 safewater Safe water               double          54     32

summ()

Summarise selected numeric variables in mtcars.

summ(mtcars, mpg, wt)
#>   name type  n unique    min     mean        sd    max
#> 1  mpg  dbl 32     25 10.400 20.09062 6.0269481 33.900
#> 2   wt  dbl 32     29  1.513  3.21725 0.9784574  5.424

Choose numeric variables deliberately: means and standard deviations of factor codes may have no substantive interpretation. Numeric and logical columns with no observed values are retained: n and unique are zero and summary statistics are NA, including sum.

Select statistics with .stat. Aliases missing, p25, p50, and p75 retain their requested names and order; sum is available for numeric summaries. Unsupported statistics produce an error. See the migration guide for the date/datetime restrictions and cross-tabulation naming rules.

summ(mtcars, mpg, .stat = c("missing", "p50", "sum"))
#>   type missing  p50   sum
#> 1  dbl       0 19.2 642.9

With .type = "table", numeric and calendar summaries share character columns for formatted statistics; counts remain numeric. Default list mode preserves numeric statistic types in the numeric summary.

tab()

Tabulate a single variable:

tab(dplyr::starwars, sex)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 6
#>   sex                n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>          <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 female            16   18.4   18.4 19.3       19.3
#> 2 hermaphroditic     1    1.15  19.5  1.20      20.5
#> 3 male              60   69.0   88.5 72.3       92.8
#> 4 none               6    6.90  95.4  7.23     100  
#> 5 <NA>               4    4.60 100   NA         NA

tab1() tabulates variables one by one as a list, and varlist() can select variables in a Stata style.

tab1(dplyr::starwars, varlist("*color"))

#>    value             n percent    cum valid valid_cum

One-way tabulation also counts list-column values. Selecting no variables returns an empty result; tab1() and fre1() return empty lists by default. Matrix columns are unsupported.

tab2() cross-tabulates two variables.

tab2(dplyr::starwars, sex, gender)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 4
#>   `sex \\ gender` feminine masculine  `NA`
#>   <chr>              <int>     <int> <int>
#> 1 female                16         0     0
#> 2 hermaphroditic         0         1     0
#> 3 male                   0        60     0
#> 4 none                   1         5     0
#> 5 <NA>                   0         0     4

fre()

fre() family functions simply add total rows (and total columns in fre2()) to their tab() counterparts.

fre() and fre2() default to .type = "auto", preserving the input container. fre1() returns a list whose tables preserve that container. Request .type = "tibble" explicitly when a tibble is required.

fre(dplyr::starwars, sex)
#> # A tibble: 7 x 6
#>   sex                n percent   cum  valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>          <int>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 female            16   18.4   18.4  19.3       19.3
#> 2 hermaphroditic     1    1.15  19.5   1.20      20.5
#> 3 male              60   69.0   88.5  72.3       92.8
#> 4 none               6    6.90  95.4   7.23     100  
#> 5 Valid Total       83   95.4   NA   100         NA  
#> 6 <NA>               4    4.60 100    NA         NA  
#> 7 Total             87  100     NA    NA         NA

For optional rich formatting, install flextable and request it explicitly:

fre(dplyr::starwars, sex, .type = "flextable")

Row calculations and binning

Row helpers return vectors that can be used in mutate():

tibble(a = c(1, NA, 3), b = c(3, NA, 5)) |>
  mutate(row_average = row_mean(a, b))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>       a     b row_average
#>   <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1     1     3           2
#> 2    NA    NA          NA
#> 3     3     5           4

xtile() keeps equal values in the same group. Ties can reduce the number of intervals, with a warning, rather than splitting equal values by row order.
